title: Webflow Development
subtitle: Plan, build and hand off responsive, CMS-powered client websites in Webflow, and price the work professionally.
description: An advanced, practical course for builders who want to deliver professional client websites in Webflow. You will master structure, classes and responsive layout, build a client-proof CMS, run launch checks for speed, accessibility and SEO, and learn the discovery, pricing and handoff skills that turn builds into paid work.
outcomes: Build clean, well-named Webflow pages using the box model, Flexbox and Grid that work at every breakpoint
Plan a site with a sitemap, content model and style guide, and build CMS Collections with templates, filters and references
Run a pre-launch check for speed, accessibility, forms and SEO, and connect a custom domain
Lead a client discovery call and turn it into a signed brief
Price a project from an hours estimate, write a scoped proposal and manage change requests
Hand off a site the client can update, and write an honest case study
audience: Women who already build simple websites or designs and want to offer professional Webflow development to local and international clients.
tools: A laptop or desktop computer with Chrome (the Webflow Designer is not built for phones)
An Android or iPhone for real-device testing

modules.title: Webflow Foundations: Platform, Structure and Responsive Layout
modules.overview: Understand where Webflow fits among website platforms and what clients actually pay for. Then master the technical core: the box model, clean page structure, class naming, and responsive layout with Flexbox, Grid and breakpoints.

lessons.title: Where Webflow fits: platforms, plans and the client work it suits
objectives: Describe what Webflow is and what the Designer, CMS and hosting each do
Compare Webflow with WordPress, Wix and hand-coded sites for a given client
Explain the difference between a Workspace plan and a Site plan
Decide when Webflow is the wrong tool and say why

blocks.text: Webflow is a website platform where you design visually but the result is real HTML, CSS and JavaScript. When you drag a box onto the canvas and give it padding, Webflow writes the CSS rule for you. That is the big difference from simple drag-and-drop builders: in Webflow you are working with the same building blocks a front-end developer types by hand, so you need to understand them. This course assumes you already use a computer comfortably and have built at least a simple page somewhere before.

blocks.name: website-builder
blocks.alt: A person arranging blocks of a web page on a large screen
blocks.caption: In Webflow you arrange real page elements visually, and Webflow writes the code underneath.

blocks.text: The three parts you will use every day

items: **The Designer**: the visual workspace where you build pages, set styles, make layouts responsive and add interactions. It runs in a desktop browser such as Chrome. It is not built for phones, so plan to work on a laptop.

**The CMS (Content Management System)**: databases called Collections, for content that repeats in the same shape, such as blog posts, menu items, properties or team members. Clients can add items without touching your design.
**Hosting**: Webflow serves the finished site. Every project gets a free staging address ending in webflow.io. Connecting a real domain such as yourbusiness.com.ng needs a paid Site plan.

blocks.text: Workspace plans and Site plans

Webflow charges in two separate ways, and clients often confuse them. A **Workspace plan** is for you, the builder: it controls how many projects you can keep, whether you can export code, and how many people can work with you. A **Site plan** is for each live website: it controls the custom domain, CMS item limits, form submissions and traffic. A common professional setup is that you hold a Workspace plan, build the site, then the client pays for their own Site plan so the website is legally and financially theirs. Prices are set in US dollars and change from time to time, so always check webflow.com/pricing on the day you quote.

blocks.title: Dollar billing in Nigeria
blocks.text: Webflow bills by card in US dollars. Many Nigerian bank cards have limits on foreign currency spending that change often. Before you promise a launch date, confirm that you or the client has a card that can make the payment, for example a dollar card from a bank or fintech app. Never pay a client's hosting with your own card without a written agreement on repayment.
How Webflow compares with the other options

head: Option
Strong at
Weak at
Good fit
rows: Custom design, clean code, built-in CMS and hosting, client editing
Dollar billing, learning curve, limited payment gateways for Nigerian online stores
Brochure sites, portfolios, landing pages, blogs, directories
Huge plugin choice, local hosting paid in naira, WooCommerce with Paystack plugins
Plugin updates, security patching, speed depends on setup
Online shops in Nigeria, sites with many special features
Very fast to start, simple editing
Less control over structure and code
Tiny budgets, owners who want to build it themselves
Client cannot edit content without a developer

blocks.text: Notice the shop problem. Webflow's own Ecommerce checkout works with Stripe and PayPal. Stripe does not list Nigeria as a supported country for direct accounts, so a Lagos fashion brand that wants naira card payments will usually be better served by a WordPress and WooCommerce shop with a Paystack plugin, or by a Webflow site whose Buy buttons link to a Paystack or Flutterwave payment page. Saying this honestly at the start saves you from a project that cannot launch.
Where the work is

Webflow client work falls into a few repeating types: marketing sites for service businesses (law firms, clinics, schools, consultants), landing pages for campaigns and events, portfolio sites for creatives, and content sites with a blog or resource library. Abroad, many agencies and start-ups hire Webflow developers remotely through platforms such as Upwork and Contra, or through the Webflow community and its partner directory. At home, the opening is businesses whose website is out of date, broken on phones, or missing completely. You do not need statistics to see this: search Google Maps for any service in your area and open ten business websites on your phone. Count how many load slowly, have broken layouts or have no site at all.

blocks.title: Choosing a platform for a client
items: Needs online card payments?
Naira checkout: WordPress or Paystack link
Content changes often?
Yes: Webflow with CMS
Simple and fixed: lighter tool
blocks.caption: Ask about payments and editing needs first, because those two answers rule out the wrong platform fastest.

blocks.title: Worked example: three enquiries, three answers
blocks.context: For example, Amaka is a Webflow freelancer in Port Harcourt. In one week she receives three enquiries on WhatsApp.
steps: A law firm wants a five-page site with a news section partners can update. Payments are not needed. Amaka recommends Webflow with one CMS Collection for news.

A shoe seller wants 200 products with naira card checkout and stock tracking. Amaka explains that Webflow Ecommerce uses Stripe and PayPal, then refers her to a WordPress developer friend, and offers to design the landing page only.

A church wants a single event page live in four days, with a registration form. Amaka builds a one-page Webflow landing page with a native form and publishes it on the client's domain on a basic Site plan.
She keeps a short note of why she said yes or no to each, to reuse in future replies.
blocks.result: Two paid Webflow projects, one goodwill referral, and no promise she could not keep.

blocks.text: Webflow skill is worth most when you combine it with design judgement and clear business conversations. The rest of this course follows that path: first the technical foundations (structure, classes and responsive layout), then the professional workflow (planning, CMS, interactions and quality checks), and finally consulting, pricing and handoff, so that at the end you can deliver a complete client site.

takeaways: Webflow is visual, but you are building real HTML and CSS, so the underlying concepts matter.
Workspace plans pay for you as the builder; Site plans pay for each live website.
Ask about online payments early: Webflow Ecommerce relies on Stripe and PayPal.
Saying no or referring a client is a professional answer when Webflow is the wrong fit.

activity.title: Platform fit audit
steps: On your phone, search Google Maps for one type of business in your area, for example dental clinics or event centres.
Open the websites of 8 to 10 of them and note: loads in under about 5 seconds or not, readable on the phone or not, has a contact form or WhatsApp link or not.
For each business, write one line: would Webflow suit them, and why or why not (think about payments and content updates).
Open webflow.com/pricing and write down today's Site plan names and what each includes.
activity.evidence: A one-page table of 8 to 10 businesses with your platform recommendation for each, plus your notes from the pricing page with today's date.

lessons.title: The box model, page structure and class naming
objectives: Explain content, padding, border and margin and calculate an element's total width
Build a clean structure of Section, Container and Div Block elements
Use classes and combo classes correctly instead of styling one element at a time
Apply a consistent naming system such as Client-First

blocks.text: Every element on a web page is a rectangle. A heading, a button, an image and the box that holds them are all boxes. The **box model** describes the layers of each box, from the inside out: the **content**, then **padding** (space inside the edge), then the **border**, then **margin** (space outside the edge, pushing other boxes away). In Webflow's Style panel you will find these under Spacing and Borders. If you understand these four layers, most layout problems stop being mysterious.

blocks.name: design-components
blocks.alt: Designer arranging interface blocks and components
blocks.caption: Every element is a box, and pages are boxes nested inside boxes.

blocks.title: Worked example: why the card is too wide
blocks.context: For example, Tolu sets a service card to width 300px, padding 24px on each side and a 1px border. Three cards in a row with 20px gaps overflow her 960px container.
steps: With the default box sizing called content-box, width means the content only. Total card width = 300 + 24 + 24 + 1 + 1 = 350px.
Three cards and two gaps: 350 x 3 + 20 x 2 = 1,050 + 40 = 1,090px, which is 130px wider than 960px.
Webflow's default styles set box-sizing to border-box, where width includes padding and border. With border-box the card is exactly 300px, so the row is 300 x 3 + 40 = 940px and fits.
Tolu checks the Style panel and finds an old custom code embed that changed box-sizing. She removes it and the row fits.
blocks.result: Knowing which box-sizing applies tells you how to add widths correctly: 940px fits inside 960px, 1,090px does not.

blocks.text: A clean page structure

Professional Webflow builds follow a predictable nesting pattern. Open the **Navigator** panel and you should see a tidy tree, not a pile of unnamed Div Blocks. A common pattern is: Body, then a **Section** for each band of the page (hero, services, testimonials, footer), then a **Container** that limits the width and centres the content, then Div Blocks, Grids or Flex boxes for the layout, then the text, images and buttons.

blocks.title: How a Webflow page nests
items: Body
Section: one band of page
Container: max width, centred
Layout wrapper: flex or grid
Content: heading, text, image
blocks.caption: Each level has one job, so you can change spacing or width in one place without breaking the rest.

items: **Section** sets top and bottom padding and the background colour of a band.
**Container** sets a maximum width, for example 1200px, and centres it with automatic left and right margins.
**Layout wrapper** decides how children sit: side by side (flex), in a grid, or stacked.
**Content elements** carry typography and images. Use real headings (H1 to H6) in order, not paragraphs made big.

blocks.text: Classes, combo classes and why they matter

In Webflow you style elements by giving them a **class**, which is a reusable named style. Give five buttons the class button and change its colour once: all five update. A **combo class** adds a variation on top of a base class, for example button plus is-secondary for an outline version. The base styles stay shared; only the differences live in the combo class. If you instead style each button separately, you create dozens of near-identical classes and the site becomes painful to change.

blocks.title: Global styles first
blocks.text: Before building any section, style the tags themselves: Body (font, size, colour), H1 to H6, Paragraph, Links and lists. Select the element, then choose the tag in the selector field rather than adding a class. Every new element then looks right by default, and you only add classes for real differences.
A naming system you can hand to a client

Names should tell the next person what an element is. Many Webflow professionals use **Client-First**, a free naming convention published by Finsweet. In Client-First, custom classes describe the component and the element with an underscore, such as header_component or services_card, while utility classes describe one job, such as padding-section-large or text-align-center. Whether you adopt Client-First fully or not, pick one system and use it for the whole project.

head: Poor name
Better name
Why
rows: Says which section and what it is
Reusable, not tied to one place
Base class plus combo for the variation
Describes the width, not the order it was made

blocks.text: Clean structure is not just tidiness. A clear Navigator tree makes responsive fixes faster, keeps the CSS file smaller (which helps loading speed), and lets the client or another developer find things months later. When you take over a messy Webflow project, budget time to clean classes before adding features; the Style Manager panel lets you find and remove unused classes. Also avoid styling with IDs or one-off classes like hero-heading-2-fix; each one is a small debt that someone has to pay later when the design changes.

takeaways: Content, padding, border, margin: every element is a box with these four layers.
With border-box sizing, width includes padding and border, which keeps arithmetic simple.
Use Section, Container, layout wrapper, content as a predictable structure.
Style tags globally first, then use classes and combo classes for variations.
Name classes by meaning, using one system such as Client-First.

activity.title: Build and name a hero section
steps: Create a free Webflow account and a blank site.
Style the Body, H1, H2 and Paragraph tags with one font and sizes of your choice.
Build a hero: Section, Container (max width 1200px), a wrapper holding an H1, a paragraph and two buttons.
Give the buttons a base class button and the second one a combo class is-secondary with an outline style.
Name every element meaningfully and take a screenshot of the Navigator panel.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your Navigator tree and the published webflow.io link of the hero section.

lessons.title: Responsive layout with Flexbox, Grid and breakpoints
objectives: Choose between Flexbox and Grid for a given layout
Explain how styles cascade across Webflow breakpoints
Calculate column widths and choose units such as rem, % and vw
Fix the most common mobile layout problems

blocks.text: Most visitors to a Nigerian small business website arrive on a phone, often over mobile data. A layout that looks perfect on your laptop but breaks on a 360px-wide Android screen is a failed layout. Webflow gives you two layout tools, **Flexbox** and **Grid**, and a set of **breakpoints** to adjust the design for smaller screens.

blocks.name: responsive
blocks.alt: The same web page shown on a laptop, tablet and phone
blocks.caption: One design, adjusted at each breakpoint so it reads well on every screen.

blocks.text: Flexbox: one direction at a time

Set an element's display to **Flex** and its children line up in a row or a column. You control direction (horizontal or vertical), alignment (start, centre, end, stretch), justification (space between, centre and so on), wrapping, and the **gap** between children. Flexbox is ideal for navigation bars, button groups, a row of icons, or a card whose button should sit at the bottom.
Grid: rows and columns together

Set display to **Grid** when you need control in two directions at once: a three-column services area, a photo gallery, or a layout where one item spans two columns. In Webflow you set the number of columns and rows, their sizes in fr units (fractions of the free space), and the gaps. Children can be placed automatically or positioned manually on specific cells.

blocks.title: Flexbox or Grid?
items: Flexbox
Grid
blocks.caption: Use Flexbox for a line of things and Grid for a two-dimensional arrangement.

blocks.text: How Webflow breakpoints cascade

Webflow's main breakpoint is **Desktop**, and that is where you design first. Styles set on Desktop cascade **down** to Tablet (991px and below), Mobile landscape (767px and below) and Mobile portrait (478px and below). A change made on Tablet affects Tablet and the smaller sizes, but never Desktop. Optional larger breakpoints (1280px, 1440px and 1920px) cascade **up** from Desktop. So the rule is: set the general style on Desktop, then override only what must change on smaller screens.

blocks.title: Worked example: a services grid from desktop to phone
blocks.context: For example, Zainab is building a catering company site. The services section has six cards in a container of max width 1140px, with a 24px gap.
steps: Desktop: grid with 3 equal columns (1fr 1fr 1fr). Card width = (1140 - 2 x 24) / 3 = 1092 / 3 = 364px.
Tablet (991px and below): she changes the grid to 2 columns. In a 940px-wide container: (940 - 24) / 2 = 458px per card.
Mobile landscape (767px and below): she changes to 1 column, so each card fills the container width.
She reduces section padding from 96px top and bottom on Desktop to 64px on Tablet and 48px on Mobile portrait, so phone users scroll less.
She previews at 360px width and finds a heading overflowing; she lowers the H2 font size on Mobile portrait only.
blocks.result: Six readable cards on every screen, achieved with four overrides instead of four separate layouts.

blocks.text: Units that adapt

head: Unit
Means
Use it for
rows: Multiple of the root font size (16px by default in browsers, so 1.5rem = 24px)
Font sizes and spacing that respect user text settings
Percentage of the screen width or height
Full-screen hero sections; use with care on phones
Fraction of the free space in a grid

blocks.title: Common phone problems and fixes
blocks.text: Horizontal scrolling on phones usually means one element is wider than the screen: a fixed width in px, a long word or URL, or an image without max width 100%. Set max-width instead of width, use % or rem, and check each section on Mobile portrait. Text set in vw can become tiny on phones, so give it a minimum using rem.
Navbars, images and text on small screens

Three elements cause most mobile trouble. The **Navbar** component in Webflow has a setting for the breakpoint at which the links collapse into a menu button; pick the size where the links stop fitting, usually Tablet, and style the open menu so links are large enough to tap. **Images** should sit inside wrappers with a set aspect ratio or height, and use object fit cover, so a portrait photo uploaded later does not stretch the card. **Text** needs a readable size on phones: body text around 1rem, and headings reduced step by step so a long H1 does not break into one word per line.

items: Tap targets: buttons and links at least about 44px tall on mobile so thumbs can hit them.
Line length: limit paragraph width on Desktop (for example max width 40rem) so lines stay comfortable to read.
Hidden elements: avoid hiding important content on mobile; if it matters on Desktop, it usually matters on a phone.

blocks.text: A good habit is to check all four main breakpoints after finishing each section, not at the end of the whole site. Fixing one section at a time takes minutes; fixing a whole site at the end can take days. Finally, the Webflow preview is a simulation: open the staging link on at least one real Android phone before you call a section done.

takeaways: Flexbox handles one direction; Grid handles rows and columns together.
Design on Desktop first; changes cascade down to Tablet and the mobile sizes.
Override only what must change on smaller screens.
Prefer max-width, %, rem and fr over fixed pixel widths.
Check each section on a real phone, not only in preview.

activity.title: Make a section fully responsive
steps: Build a features section with six cards in a 3-column Grid on Desktop.
Change it to 2 columns on Tablet and 1 column on Mobile landscape.
Reduce the section padding and H2 size on smaller breakpoints.
Build a navbar row with Flexbox: logo left, links right, space between.
Publish and open the link on a real phone; record any problem you fix.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of the section at all four breakpoints plus a short note of each fix you made after the phone test.

quiz.q: A card is set to width 280px with 20px padding on each side and a 2px border, using content-box sizing. What is its total width?
quiz.explain: Content-box adds padding and border to the width: 280 + 20 + 20 + 2 + 2 = 324px. With border-box it would be exactly 280px.

quiz.q: Chioma changes a heading's font size while on the Tablet breakpoint. Where does the change show?
options: Tablet and all smaller breakpoints, not Desktop
quiz.explain: In Webflow, styles cascade down from the breakpoint where you set them. Tablet changes affect Tablet, Mobile landscape and Mobile portrait.

quiz.q: A law firm needs a news section the partners can update themselves. What should the developer use?
options: A separate static page for every article
A CMS Collection for news items with a template page
A custom code embed for each article
quiz.explain: Repeating content in the same shape belongs in a CMS Collection, which the client can update without touching the design.

quiz.q: You need a gallery where one photo spans two columns. Which layout is the better choice?
quiz.explain: Grid controls rows and columns together and lets an item span several cells.

quiz.q: A Lagos shop wants 150 products with naira card payments at checkout. What is the honest first answer?
options: Webflow Ecommerce will handle naira cards directly
Webflow Ecommerce uses Stripe and PayPal, so consider WooCommerce with Paystack or Paystack payment links
Any website builder works the same for payments
Payments are not possible online in Nigeria
quiz.explain: Payment gateway support decides the platform. Webflow Ecommerce relies on Stripe and PayPal, so a naira checkout usually needs another route.

quiz.q: Five buttons share the class button. Two need an outline style. What is the cleanest approach?
options: Add a combo class such as is-secondary to the two buttons
Use custom code for those two
Change the base class to outline
quiz.explain: A combo class stores only the differences, while the shared base class keeps the common styles in one place.

modules.title: Professional Build Workflow: Planning, CMS and Launch
modules.overview: Move from a brief to a launched site the way professionals do. You will plan sitemaps and content models, build a client-proof CMS, then add interactions and forms and run speed, accessibility and SEO checks before connecting the domain.

lessons.title: Planning a client site: sitemap, content model and style guide
objectives: Turn a client brief into a sitemap of static pages and CMS template pages
Write a content model listing each Collection and its fields
Set up a style guide page with variables for colours, type and spacing
Estimate build effort from the plan before opening the Designer

blocks.text: Advanced Webflow developers spend real time planning before they build. Rebuilding a section because the content did not fit is far more expensive than an hour with a notebook or a Google Doc. The plan has three parts: a **sitemap** (which pages exist), a **content model** (which content repeats and what fields it needs), and a **style guide** (the design decisions every page will reuse).

blocks.name: content-structure
blocks.alt: Person arranging blocks of content into a structured layout
blocks.caption: Planning the content structure first tells you which pages are static and which come from the CMS.

blocks.text: Static pages and CMS template pages

A **static page** is designed once and holds content that rarely changes: Home, About, Contact. A **Collection template page** is designed once but displays any item from a CMS Collection, so one template can produce 5 or 500 pages, each with its own address such as /projects/lekki-duplex. When you draw the sitemap, mark which is which. If a client says 'we will add a new one every month', that content belongs in the CMS.

blocks.title: From brief to build plan
items: Client brief
Sitemap: static vs template
Content model: fields
Style guide and variables
Build in order
blocks.caption: Each step feeds the next, so the build itself becomes assembly rather than guessing.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning an interior design studio site
blocks.context: For example, Funmi runs an interior design studio in Abuja and wants a site to show projects, list services and get enquiries. She adds about two projects a month.
steps: Static pages: Home, About, Services, Contact. That is 4 pages to design.
CMS Collections: Projects (repeats monthly) and Testimonials (shown on several pages).

Projects fields: Name (plain text), Slug (automatic), Location (plain text), Cover image (image), Gallery (multi-image), Summary (plain text, under 160 characters), Story (rich text), Project type (option: Residential, Office, Hospitality), Featured (switch).
Testimonials fields: Client first name, Quote, Related project (reference to Projects).
Template pages: 1, the Project template. Total unique designs: 4 static + 1 template = 5, even though the site may grow to 50 project pages.
blocks.result: A one-page plan showing 5 designs to build and 2 Collections, which the developer uses both to estimate time and to explain the site to the client.

blocks.text: Choosing field types well

head: Field type
Use for
Watch out
rows: No formatting; set a character limit for summaries
Long articles with headings, lists and images
Style the Rich Text element so client content looks right
Ask for a minimum size and landscape or portrait
A fixed list such as project type
Good for filtering; clients cannot add new options themselves
Yes or no, such as Featured
Use it to filter lists, for example featured projects on Home
Plan these early; they are harder to add later

blocks.text: The style guide page and variables

Create a hidden page called Style Guide before any real page. On it, place every heading level, paragraph sizes, buttons, form fields, links and colour samples, all using your global tag styles and classes. Then use Webflow **Variables** (in the Variables panel) to store design values with names: colours such as brand-primary and text-dark, sizes such as space-medium, and font families. When the client changes brand colour, you change one variable and the whole site updates.

items: Colours: brand-primary, brand-secondary, text-dark, text-light, background-light, border.
Type scale: for example H1 3rem, H2 2.25rem, H3 1.5rem, body 1rem, small 0.875rem (at a 16px root, H1 is 48px).
Spacing: space-small 1rem, space-medium 2rem, section padding 6rem on Desktop.
Buttons: primary, secondary and text-link styles, each with hover and focus states.

blocks.title: Get real content early
blocks.text: Ask for the client's real text and photos before you build. Placeholder text hides problems: a Yoruba business name that is longer than your sample, or a client photo in portrait when you designed for landscape. If content is late, agree in writing that the timeline moves with it.
Using the plan to estimate

Once you know the number of unique designs and Collections, estimation becomes realistic. Keep your own records from practice projects: for example, how many hours a static page, a template page and a Collection setup each took you, including responsive fixes. Add time for content entry, testing and client revisions. Your personal numbers are more useful than any figure from the internet, because they reflect your speed and your tools.

Share the sitemap and content model with the client for approval before building. A signed-off plan becomes the baseline for scope: if the client later asks for an Events Collection, you can show that it was not in the approved plan and quote it separately, which you will practise in Module 3.

takeaways: Plan the sitemap, the content model and the style guide before building.
Content that repeats belongs in a CMS Collection with one template page.
Choose field types carefully; references are hard to add later.
Variables let one change update colours, sizes and fonts site-wide.
An approved plan is your baseline for scope and estimates.

activity.title: Write a build plan
steps: Pick a real local business type, for example a school, clinic or caterer.
Draw its sitemap and mark static pages and template pages.
Write the content model: each Collection with field names and types.
Build a Style Guide page in Webflow using at least 6 colour variables and a type scale.
Count the unique designs and write your estimated hours for each.
activity.evidence: Your sitemap and content model document, plus a screenshot of the Style Guide page and the Variables panel.

lessons.title: CMS in depth: Collections, template pages, lists and filters
objectives: Create a Collection with the right fields and add items
Design a Collection template page with dynamic bindings
Show filtered and sorted Collection Lists on static pages
Connect Collections with reference fields and import items by CSV

blocks.text: The CMS is what makes a Webflow site sustainable for a client. Done well, the client adds a new project or blog post in a few minutes and it appears in the right places, in the right style, automatically. Done badly, the client breaks the layout or calls you for every change. This lesson walks through a full CMS setup.

blocks.name: organized-content
blocks.alt: Content cards neatly organised into groups
blocks.caption: A Collection keeps repeating content in one consistent structure.

blocks.text: Step by step: from Collection to live pages

items: Open the CMS panel and create a Collection, for example Projects. Webflow adds Name and Slug fields automatically.
Add the fields from your content model, mark the essential ones as required, and add help text that tells the client what to enter, for example 'Landscape photo, at least 1600px wide'.
Add three to five real items so you can design with true content lengths.

Open the Collection template page. Add elements and connect each to a field using the 'Get text from' or 'Get image from' settings. The heading shows the project name, the image shows the cover, and so on.
On a static page such as Home, add a Collection List, connect it to Projects, and design one item; every other item copies that design.
Set filters and sorting in the Collection List settings, and limit how many items appear.

blocks.title: How CMS content flows
items: Client adds item
Item fills template page
Lists update on static pages
Visitors see new content
Client adds the next
blocks.caption: You design once; after that, the client's new items flow through the site without your help.

blocks.text: Filters, sorting and conditional visibility

Collection List settings let you filter by field values, for example show only items where Featured is on, or where Project type equals Residential. You can sort by a field, such as newest date first, and limit the list to a number of items, such as the latest 3 on the Home page. **Conditional visibility** hides an element when a field is empty or meets a condition, so a 'Watch video' button disappears on projects that have no video link instead of showing a broken link.

blocks.title: Worked example: featured projects and a related list
blocks.context: For example, Halima is finishing the interior studio site from the planning lesson, with 12 projects and 6 testimonials already entered.
steps: Home page: a Collection List of Projects, filter Featured is On, sort by a Completed date field she added, newest first, limit 3 items. Of 12 projects, 4 are featured, so the newest 3 of those 4 show.
Project template page: a second Collection List of Projects, filtered to the same Project type as the current page and excluding the current item, limited to 2, labelled 'More like this'.
Testimonials: each testimonial references a project. On the project template she adds a Collection List of Testimonials filtered to those whose Related project equals the current project.
She sets conditional visibility so the testimonial block is hidden when a project has no testimonial.
She tests by switching Featured off on one item and confirms the Home list changes after publishing.
blocks.result: The client controls what appears on Home with a single switch, and each project page shows relevant extra content without manual linking.

blocks.text: Moving content in bulk

When a client already has content, for example 80 products in an Excel sheet or posts on an old site, use **CSV import**. Save the sheet as CSV, make sure the column names map to your fields, and import from the Collection settings. Webflow lets you match columns to fields before importing. Images in a CSV must be public URLs. Test with five rows first, check the template pages, then import the rest. You can also export a Collection to CSV as a backup.

blocks.title: Know the plan limits
blocks.text: Each Site plan has a limit on the number of CMS items and Collections. Count the client's current items and expected growth, for example 30 posts now and 4 a month is about 78 after a year, and check the limits on webflow.com/pricing before recommending a plan.
Making the CMS client-proof

items: Write help text on every field so the client knows sizes, lengths and formats.
Style every element inside the Rich Text block (H2, H3, lists, images, quotes) so pasted content still looks designed.
Use Option fields for categories instead of free text, so 'Residential' never becomes 'residental'.
Set character limits on summaries so cards do not break.
Remember that code export does not include working CMS features, so a CMS site should stay hosted on Webflow.

blocks.text: Test the CMS the way a client will use it: open the site in Editor mode, add an item with a very long title and one with no image, and see what breaks. Fix it now, because the client will do exactly this in the first month.

takeaways: Design the template page once and connect elements to fields.
Collection Lists can filter, sort and limit items on any page.
Reference fields and conditional visibility create related, tidy content.
Use CSV import for bulk content, testing a few rows first.
Help text, Option fields and styled Rich Text keep the CMS client-proof.

activity.title: Build a working CMS feature
steps: Create a Collection with at least 6 fields, including an image, an option and a switch.
Add 6 real or realistic items, one with a very long name and one with no image.
Design the template page with all fields connected and one conditional element.
Add a filtered, sorted, limited Collection List to the home page.
Import 5 more items from a CSV file you prepared in Google Sheets.
activity.evidence: The staging link, a screenshot of the Collection fields with help text, and the CSV file you imported.

lessons.title: Interactions, forms, performance, accessibility and launch
objectives: Add purposeful interactions without hurting usability
Set up forms responsibly, including spam protection and data privacy
Run a pre-launch check for speed, accessibility and SEO
Connect a custom domain and publish safely

blocks.text: This lesson takes a finished build to a live, professional site. It covers the last layers clients notice (movement and forms) and the ones they do not notice until they go wrong (speed, accessibility, search settings and the domain).

blocks.name: launching
blocks.alt: A rocket launching from a laptop screen
blocks.caption: Launch is a checklist, not a single click on Publish.

blocks.text: Interactions with a purpose

Webflow's Interactions panel connects a **trigger** (mouse click, hover, an element scrolling into view, page load or page scroll) to **actions** such as move, fade (opacity), scale or show and hide. Good uses: a mobile menu opening, an FAQ answer expanding, a gentle fade-in of cards as they scroll into view. Poor uses: long animations that delay reading, text that only appears after hovering (phones cannot hover), or heavy effects that slow cheaper phones. Keep most animations short, around 0.2 to 0.5 seconds, and make sure content is readable even if an animation does not run.
Forms that work and respect privacy

items: Use Webflow's form block; submissions appear in the site's Forms settings and can be emailed to the client.
Give every field a visible label, not only placeholder text, and mark which fields are required.
Turn on reCAPTCHA in the form settings to reduce spam.

Collect only what you need. If the form asks for names, phone numbers or emails, add a short privacy note and a link to a privacy policy. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets duties for anyone processing personal data; the client should take advice on their obligations.
Test every form on the live domain and confirm the client actually receives the notification email.

blocks.text: Speed checks

Run the staging link through **PageSpeed Insights** (pagespeed.web.dev), which uses Google's Lighthouse. Look at the mobile result first. The most common Webflow speed problem is oversized images: a 5MB photo straight from a phone. Resize images before upload (a hero rarely needs to be wider than about 2000px), use modern formats such as WebP, which Webflow can convert in the Assets panel, and keep images below the first screen on lazy loading. Avoid many large custom fonts and heavy third-party scripts.

blocks.title: Worked example: cutting page weight
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma's home page loads slowly on mobile. PageSpeed Insights flags 6 images totalling about 14MB.
steps: She resizes the hero from 6000px wide to 2000px and converts it to WebP: from about 5MB to about 300KB.
She resizes 5 card photos to 1000px wide and converts them: from about 9MB in total to about 600KB.
New total for images: 0.3 + 0.6 = 0.9MB, against 14MB before, a saving of about 13.1MB, roughly 94 percent.
She sets the card images to lazy load and keeps the hero image on eager load.
She re-runs PageSpeed Insights and records the before and after scores in her QA sheet.
blocks.result: A visitor on mobile data downloads under 1MB of images instead of 14MB, which matters a great deal when data is expensive.

blocks.text: Accessibility checks

items: Colour contrast: WCAG asks for at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Check brand colours with a contrast checker before you build.
Alt text on every meaningful image (set in the Assets panel or element settings); mark decorative images as decorative.
One H1 per page and headings in order, without skipping levels for looks.
Every interactive element reachable and visible with the keyboard: press Tab through the page and watch the focus outline.
Use Webflow's Audit panel to catch missing alt text and other flagged issues.

blocks.text: SEO settings and launch

Search settings are mostly about clarity. Search engines read the page title, the headings and the text, so a services page titled 'Services' tells them little, while 'Event Catering in Abuja | Ada's Kitchen' says what the business does and where. Keep slugs short and readable, such as /services/wedding-catering, and decide them before launch, because changing a slug later breaks shared links unless you add a redirect.

blocks.title: Pre-launch checklist
items: Titles and meta descriptions set
Images resized, alt text added
Forms tested on live domain
All breakpoints and real phone checked
Redirects added for old URLs
Domain connected, SSL on
blocks.caption: Tick every item before you tell the client the site is live.

blocks.text: In each page's settings, write a unique title and meta description, and set the Open Graph image so links shared on WhatsApp show a proper preview. For CMS templates, build titles from fields, for example the project name plus the studio name. In Site settings, confirm the sitemap is generated automatically, and add **301 redirects** if the client's old site had pages at different addresses. To connect a domain bought from a registrar such as Whogohost or QServers, add the domain in Webflow's Publishing settings, then copy the DNS records Webflow shows you into the registrar's DNS panel. DNS changes can take time to spread. Keep SSL on so the site loads over https, then publish to the custom domain and test again.

takeaways: Interactions should help users, stay short and never hide essential content.
Forms need labels, spam protection, minimal data and a privacy note.
Oversized images are the most common speed problem; resize and convert them.
Check contrast, alt text, heading order and keyboard focus before launch.
Set titles, descriptions, redirects and DNS carefully, then retest on the live domain.

activity.title: Run a full pre-launch QA
steps: Add one useful interaction, such as an FAQ accordion, to your practice site.
Run PageSpeed Insights on mobile and save the score.
Fix at least three image or font issues and run the test again.
Tab through every page with the keyboard and fix any invisible focus states.
Fill in the six-item pre-launch checklist with notes for each item.
activity.evidence: A QA sheet with before and after PageSpeed scores, the completed checklist, and a screenshot of the Audit panel.

quiz.q: A client will add a new event every week. How should the events be built?
options: A new static page each week
A CMS Collection with one Event template page
One long page edited by the developer weekly
quiz.explain: Content that repeats in the same shape belongs in a Collection; one template page displays every event.

quiz.q: A 'Watch video' button shows on every project page, but only some projects have a video link. What fixes this best?
options: Conditional visibility: hide the button when the video field is empty
Ask the client to add a fake link
quiz.explain: Conditional visibility hides an element based on a field, so empty fields do not leave broken buttons.

quiz.q: Home page images total 12MB. After resizing and converting, they total 0.6MB. Roughly what share of image weight was saved?
Brand pink text on a white background measures 3.1:1 contrast. It is used for normal-size body text. What should you do?
options: Darken the text colour until it reaches at least 4.5:1
quiz.explain: WCAG asks for at least 4.5:1 for normal text; 3:1 is only enough for large text.

quiz.q: The client's old site had a page at /our-services, and the new one is /services. What should you add before launch?
options: Nothing, Google will work it out
quiz.explain: A 301 redirect sends visitors and search engines from the old address to the new one, keeping links working.

quiz.q: Which piece of planning should be agreed with the client before building, to protect scope?
options: The order you will build sections
quiz.explain: An approved sitemap and content model define what is in scope, so new Collections or pages can be quoted separately.

modules.title: Consulting, Pricing and Growing Your Webflow Practice
modules.overview: Learn the client side of Webflow work: running discovery, pricing and proposing with clear scope, and handing off a site the client can run. Finish with a case study and a 90-day plan to win paid projects in a chosen niche.

lessons.title: Client discovery: questions, goals and a written brief
objectives: Run a structured discovery call covering goals, audience, content, updates and budget
Turn answers into one measurable website goal
Spot red flags that signal scope or payment problems
Write a one-page project brief the client signs off

blocks.text: Most failed website projects fail before the first pixel: the developer built what they assumed, not what the business needed. Discovery is a structured conversation, usually 30 to 45 minutes on a call, Google Meet or WhatsApp video, that turns a vague request ('we need a new website') into a clear, written brief.

blocks.name: meeting
blocks.alt: Two people in a meeting reviewing notes together
blocks.caption: A focused discovery call gives you the facts you need to plan, price and build.

blocks.text: The five areas to cover

head: Area
Questions to ask
What the answer decides
rows: What should a visitor do on the site? How will you know it is working?
The main call to action and how success is measured
Who visits? Where are they and what device do they use?
Language, tone, mobile priority, page speed budget
Do you have text, photos and a logo ready? Who writes new content?
Timeline and whether copywriting is in scope
What will you change yourselves after launch, and how often?
What budget have you set? Is there a fixed launch date, such as an event?
Scope, plan choice and whether the project is viable

blocks.text: Ask about integrations too: booking tools such as Calendly, WhatsApp chat links, email newsletters such as Mailchimp or Brevo, Google Analytics, payment links. Each one adds time. Ask who owns the domain today and who can log in to it; lost domain logins are one of the most common causes of launch delays.
From wishes to one measurable goal

Clients often list features: a slider, a blog, animations, a chatbot. Bring the conversation back to the business result. A useful website goal names an action and a measure, for example: 'Increase enquiry form submissions from about 5 a month to 15 a month within 3 months of launch.' The goal then guides decisions. If a feature does not help that goal, it can wait for phase two.

blocks.title: Worked example: discovery with a private school
blocks.context: For example, Grace runs discovery with the administrator of a private primary school in Ibadan that wants a new website before admissions open in 10 weeks.
steps: Goal: more admission enquiries. Today the school gets about 8 a month through phone calls; the target is 20 a month during admission season.
Audience: parents within the city, mostly on phones, many asking questions on WhatsApp.
Content: photos exist but are low quality; the brochure text is 3 years old. Grace notes that photography and copy updates are not yet budgeted.
Updates: the school wants to post news and events weekly, so News and Events become CMS Collections.
Timeline: 10 weeks to admissions. Grace works backwards: 1 week plan, 4 weeks build, 1 week content entry, 1 week testing and training, leaving 3 weeks buffer for content delays.
blocks.result: A clear brief with one measurable goal, two Collections, a content gap flagged early, and a realistic schedule with buffer.

blocks.title: Discovery to approved brief
items: Enquiry and short form
Discovery call
Written brief
Client feedback
Signed brief
blocks.caption: Nothing is designed until the brief is signed, so everyone agrees on the target first.

blocks.text: Red flags to notice

items: No budget at all, or 'we will pay when we start making money from the site'.
A launch date that leaves no time for content: the site cannot go live without text and photos.
Several decision-makers with no single person who approves work.
A request to copy a competitor's site exactly, including their text or photos, which raises copyright problems.
Pressure to start immediately without a deposit or written agreement.

blocks.title: Protect logins and data
blocks.text: Never ask a client to send passwords in a WhatsApp group or email. Ask them to invite you to their Webflow Site, domain registrar or Google account as a collaborator, or to type the login themselves during a call. Use a password manager for any access you must hold, and remove your access after handoff.
Listening well on the call

Let the client talk more than you do. Ask open questions ('Tell me about the last three customers who found you online') and follow up with 'Why is that important?' until you reach the business reason. Take notes in the client's own words, because those words often become the headline on the home page. Before the call ends, read back the goal and the main points and ask, 'Did I miss anything?' Finally, agree the next step and date, for example 'I will send the brief by Thursday.'

If you cannot meet live, a short Google Form with the same five areas works as a first step, followed by a 15-minute call to fill the gaps. Many busy owners in Nigeria prefer to answer by WhatsApp voice notes; that is fine, but summarise the voice notes in writing so there is a clear record.
The written brief

Within 48 hours of the call, send a one-page brief: the business and its goal with the measure, the audience, the sitemap draft, the CMS Collections, integrations, what the client provides (content, logo, photos, domain access) with dates, the launch target, and anything deliberately left out. Ask the client to reply 'approved' or sign it. This document feeds directly into your proposal in the next lesson.

takeaways: Cover goal, audience, content, updates, and budget and timeline in every discovery call.
Turn feature wishes into one measurable website goal.
Work backwards from the launch date and leave buffer for late content.
Notice red flags early, and never collect passwords over chat.
Send a one-page brief for approval before any design work.

activity.title: Practice discovery and brief
steps: Write your own discovery question list with at least 3 questions for each of the 5 areas.
Run a 30-minute practice call with a friend who owns or works in a small business.
Write a one-page brief with one measurable goal and a backwards schedule.
Ask the friend to point out anything unclear, then revise the brief.
activity.evidence: Your question list and the revised one-page brief, with the friend's feedback noted.

lessons.title: Pricing, proposals and scope control
objectives: Calculate a project price from estimated hours, rate, costs and a risk buffer
Write a proposal with clear inclusions, exclusions and payment milestones
Handle change requests with a simple change order
Separate the build fee from hosting and care plans

blocks.text: Most Webflow projects are priced as a fixed project fee, because the scope can be defined: a set number of page designs, Collections and features. A fixed price is easier for clients to approve, but it only protects you if the scope is written clearly. Pricing therefore starts with your estimate and ends with a document that says exactly what the price buys.

blocks.name: contract-signed
blocks.alt: A signed contract with a pen beside it
blocks.caption: A clear proposal and signed agreement protect both you and the client.

blocks.text: Building the price

items: List the work from the approved brief: static pages, template pages, Collections, interactions, forms, content entry, testing, training.
Estimate hours for each from your own records of practice projects.
Add project management and revisions, often a fixed share of the build time.
Multiply by your hourly rate, decided from your living costs, target income and the market you serve.
Add a risk buffer for unknowns, then round to a clean figure.
Quote hosting separately: the client pays the Webflow Site plan directly.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing the school website
blocks.context: For example, Grace prices the school site from the previous lesson. All naira figures are illustrative, not market rates; set your own rate from your costs and market.
steps: Estimate: 5 static pages x 6 hours = 30 hours; 2 template pages x 5 hours = 10 hours; 2 Collections setup and lists = 6 hours; forms and interactions = 4 hours; testing = 6 hours; client training = 2 hours. Total = 58 hours.
Project management and revisions at 20 percent: 58 x 0.2 = 11.6, rounded to 12 hours. New total = 70 hours.
At an illustrative rate of 8,000 naira an hour: 70 x 8,000 = 560,000 naira.
Risk buffer of 10 percent for content delays: 560,000 x 0.1 = 56,000. Subtotal = 616,000 naira, rounded to 620,000 naira.

Milestones: 40 percent deposit (248,000), 40 percent on design approval of the home page and template (248,000), 20 percent before publishing to the custom domain (124,000). Check: 248,000 + 248,000 + 124,000 = 620,000.
blocks.result: A price of 620,000 naira (illustrative) backed by a visible estimate, with Webflow hosting quoted separately for the school to pay directly.

blocks.text: What the proposal must say

head: Section
Example wording
rows: Increase admission enquiries through a mobile-first website.
5 page designs, News and Events Collections with templates, enquiry form, responsive on all breakpoints, basic SEO settings, 1-hour Editor training, 2 rounds of revisions per page.
Copywriting, photography, logo design, online payments, translations, content entry beyond 10 items, ongoing updates after launch.
Final text and photos by week 2, domain access, one person who approves work.
6 weeks from deposit and receipt of content.
40 / 40 / 20 milestones, by bank transfer or Paystack payment link.
Client pays the Webflow Site plan directly in US dollars; price checked on the day.

blocks.title: Handling a new request
items: Small, in scope: do it
Big, in scope: schedule it
Small, out of scope: quick quote
Big, out of scope: change order
blocks.caption: Place each new request in a quadrant before you reply, so your answer is consistent.

blocks.text: Scope control without conflict

Change requests are normal. The aim is not to refuse them but to make their cost visible. When the client asks for something outside the proposal, reply warmly, confirm what they want, and send a short **change order**: what will be added, the extra price, and how the timeline moves. Work starts when they approve it. Keeping a simple log of requests in Google Sheets helps you see when small favours have added up to days of unpaid work.

blocks.title: Payment safety
blocks.text: Take a deposit before starting and keep the site on your workspace, or unpublished from the client's domain, until the final milestone is paid; then transfer it. Confirm payments in your actual bank or Paystack dashboard, not from a screenshot, because fake transfer alerts and edited receipts are a known scam.
Setting your hourly rate

Work out the rate rather than copying someone else's. Add up your monthly business and living costs that work must cover, then divide by the hours you can realistically bill. For example, if you need 400,000 naira a month (illustrative) and can bill 80 hours (many freelancers bill only about half their working hours, because the rest goes to sales, admin and learning), your floor rate is 400,000 / 80 = 5,000 naira an hour. Then compare it with what your niche will pay and the value of the result. For clients abroad paying in dollars, research rates on the platforms you use and remember that platform fees and transfer costs reduce what you receive.

blocks.title: Put it in writing
blocks.text: Even a simple agreement helps: the proposal plus a short contract covering payment terms, ownership transfer after final payment, how many revisions are included, what happens if the client delays content for more than a set number of weeks, and that you may show the work in your portfolio.
Care plans after launch

Many clients want help after launch but not a full project. Offer an optional monthly care plan: for example, a set number of small edits, a monthly speed and form check, and priority response. Price it from the hours it really takes. It gives the client peace of mind and gives you steadier income between projects.

takeaways: Build fixed prices from estimated hours, your rate, management time and a buffer.
Write inclusions and exclusions plainly; exclusions prevent most disputes.
Use milestones and confirm payments in your real dashboard.
Answer change requests with a change order, not silent extra work.
Quote hosting separately and offer an optional care plan.

activity.title: Price and propose
steps: Take the brief from the previous activity and list every task with estimated hours.
Add 20 percent for management and revisions and a 10 percent buffer; show your arithmetic.
Write a one to two page proposal using the seven sections in the table.
Write one sample change order for a request outside the scope.
activity.evidence: Your pricing sheet with calculations, the proposal, and the sample change order.

lessons.title: Handoff, case studies and your 90-day client plan
objectives: Transfer a finished site and train the client to use the Editor
Write a case study that shows decisions and results
Choose a niche and outreach channels for Webflow work
Draft a 90-day plan with weekly actions and measures

blocks.text: A project is not finished when the site is live. It is finished when the client owns it, can update it, and would recommend you. That last part, plus a well-written case study, is how one project leads to the next.

blocks.name: portfolio-website
blocks.alt: A portfolio website displaying project cards
blocks.caption: Each finished client site becomes evidence for the next client.

blocks.text: A clean handoff

items: Confirm final payment in your bank or Paystack dashboard.
Transfer the site to the client's own Webflow workspace, or confirm they own the Site plan and invite their staff as content editors.
Record a short screen video showing how to add a CMS item, edit text and replace an image in the Editor.
Run a live 30 to 60 minute training session where the client does each task while you watch.
Send a handoff document: logins they own, Collections and what each is for, image size rules, who to call for help, and your care plan option.
Remove any access you no longer need.

blocks.title: Ask for the testimonial at the happy moment
blocks.text: The best time to ask for a review is right after training, when the client has just updated their own site for the first time. Ask two specific questions: what was the problem before, and what is different now? Specific answers make far stronger testimonials than 'great work'.
Writing a case study

A Webflow case study should prove that you think, not only that you can click. Keep it to one page on your own Webflow portfolio site. Use real numbers only if the client agrees and they are true, and never claim results you have not measured.

blocks.title: Case study structure
items: Client and goal
Problem before
Key decisions
Build highlights
Result and quote
blocks.caption: Each part answers a question a future client is quietly asking.

blocks.title: Worked example: turning the school project into a case study
blocks.context: For example, Grace finished the school site and, three months later, asked the administrator for the enquiry count with permission to publish it.
steps: Client and goal: a private primary school wanting more admission enquiries before the new session.
Problem before: an old site that broke on phones, with no way for staff to post news.
Key decisions: mobile-first layout, a WhatsApp enquiry button and a short form, News and Events as CMS Collections, images resized for mobile data.
Build highlights: screenshots of the home page on a phone, the Events template, and the Editor view staff use.

Result: the school reports enquiries rising from about 8 a month to about 18 a month during admission season, which is 10 more, or 125 percent more (10 / 8 = 1.25). She adds the administrator's quote and notes that other factors, such as their open day, also played a part.
blocks.result: An honest, specific case study with a verified result, which Grace links in every proposal she sends to schools.

blocks.text: Choosing a niche

Specialising makes you easier to find and easier to trust. A developer who has built three school sites speaks a school's language and can reuse a tested structure. Choose a niche where you have access (people you know, a sector you worked in), where clients need regular content updates (which suits the CMS), and where a website clearly affects income. Examples include schools, clinics and pharmacies, real estate firms, event venues, NGOs and consultants. For international work, niches such as SaaS start-ups or agencies that need Webflow developers are common, but competition is higher.

head: Channel
How to use it
Weekly target example
rows: Send a short, personal message with one specific fix you noticed on their current site
Ask each past client and friend to introduce you to one business
Apply only to Webflow jobs that match your niche, with a tailored first line
Post one before and after or build tip on LinkedIn or X
Answer questions in the Webflow forum and share work in the community showcase

blocks.text: Your 90-day plan

Divide the 90 days into three blocks. **Days 1 to 30**: finish two portfolio projects in your niche (a real client or a realistic concept for a named business type), publish your Webflow portfolio site and write one case study. **Days 31 to 60**: run your weekly outreach targets and track every message in a sheet. **Days 61 to 90**: follow up, refine your offer based on replies, and aim to close at least one paid project. Measure inputs you control (messages sent, proposals written) as well as results (calls booked, projects won); for example, 10 messages a week for 8 weeks is 80 conversations started. Review the sheet every Friday: which channel produced replies, and which message wording worked? Do more of what works and drop what does not.

takeaways: Handoff means the client owns the site and can update it confidently.
Train live, record a short video and leave a handoff document.
Case studies show the problem, your decisions and verified results.
A niche with frequent content updates suits Webflow's CMS.
Track weekly outreach inputs as well as projects won.

activity.title: Plan your next 90 days
steps: Choose one niche and write three reasons it suits you and Webflow.
Write a handoff document template you can reuse for every client.
Draft a one-page case study for your best practice project.
Build a 90-day plan in Google Sheets with weekly outreach targets and columns for results.
activity.evidence: Your handoff template, your case study draft and the 90-day plan sheet.

quiz.q: A client says, 'We want a slider, a chatbot and animations.' What should you do first in discovery?
options: Agree to all features and quote
Ask what visitors should do on the site and how success will be measured
quiz.explain: Features should serve a measurable goal. Clarifying the goal first lets you prioritise what really helps.

quiz.q: Estimated build time is 50 hours. You add 20 percent for management and revisions. At an illustrative rate of 10,000 naira an hour, what is the fee before any buffer?
Midway through, the client asks for an online Events booking system that was not in the proposal. What is the professional response?
options: Build it quietly to keep them happy
Send a change order with the added work, price and new timeline
Remove another page to make room
quiz.explain: Out-of-scope work is handled with a change order so the cost and time are visible and agreed.

quiz.q: A client sends a screenshot of a transfer for the final payment and asks you to transfer the site immediately. What should you do?
options: Confirm the payment has arrived in your bank or Paystack dashboard before transferring
quiz.explain: Fake alerts and edited receipts are a known scam. Only your own dashboard confirms money has arrived.

quiz.q: A school's enquiries rose from 12 to 18 a month after launch. What percentage increase can you honestly state, with permission?
quiz.explain: Increase = 18 - 12 = 6. 6 / 12 = 0.5, so 50 percent. Note that other factors may also have contributed.

quiz.q: Which item is the best example of an exclusion in a Webflow proposal?
options: Copywriting and photography are not included
Two rounds of revisions per page
quiz.explain: Exclusions state what the price does not cover. The others are inclusions.

finalQuiz.q: Which statement about Webflow is correct?
options: It only produces images of websites
It is a visual tool that produces real HTML and CSS, with a built-in CMS and hosting
It requires writing all code by hand
It cannot be used for client sites
finalQuiz.explain: Webflow writes real HTML, CSS and JavaScript from visual work and includes CMS and hosting.

finalQuiz.q: Who usually pays for the Webflow Site plan in a professional setup?
options: The client, so the site is theirs
Nobody, all sites are free with a custom domain
finalQuiz.explain: A Site plan pays for one live site; having the client pay it keeps ownership and costs clear.

finalQuiz.q: With border-box sizing, a card has width 320px, padding 24px each side and a 1px border. What is its total width?
finalQuiz.explain: Under border-box, the width already includes padding and border, so the card is 320px.

finalQuiz.q: A section looks right on Desktop but the 3-column grid is cramped on phones. What is the right fix?
options: Rebuild the section for mobile separately
Change the grid to fewer columns on smaller breakpoints
finalQuiz.explain: Override only what must change at smaller breakpoints, such as the number of grid columns.

finalQuiz.q: A container is 1,200px wide with 4 equal grid columns and 24px gaps. How wide is each column?
Which content should become a CMS Collection?
options: Team member profiles that change as staff join and leave
finalQuiz.explain: Repeating items with the same shape that change over time belong in the CMS.

finalQuiz.q: On a project template page, how do you show only projects of the same type, excluding the current one?
options: Copy and paste each project manually
A Collection List filtered by the current item's project type, excluding the current item
finalQuiz.explain: Collection List filters can reference the current item's fields, creating related lists automatically.

finalQuiz.q: A blog has 40 posts and adds 6 a month. About how many posts after one year?
finalQuiz.explain: 6 x 12 = 72 new posts. 40 + 72 = 112. Compare this with the Site plan's CMS item limit.

finalQuiz.q: Which is the best use of an interaction?
options: Text that only appears on mouse hover
A 5-second animation before the headline shows
An FAQ answer that expands on click
finalQuiz.explain: Purposeful, short interactions help users. Hover-only content fails on phones, and long animations delay reading.

finalQuiz.q: A contact form collects names and phone numbers. What should accompany it?
options: A short privacy note and a link to a privacy policy, with spam protection on
finalQuiz.explain: Collect only what is needed, explain how data is used (Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 applies to personal data) and reduce spam with reCAPTCHA.

capstone.title: Webflow Website Build Project
capstone.brief: Build a complete, responsive multi-page Webflow website for a real or realistic client in your chosen niche, including at least one CMS Collection, then document it with a case study and a pricing proposal and 90-day plan for winning Webflow work.
steps: Run a discovery conversation (with a real business or a friend playing the client) and write a signed one-page brief with one measurable goal.
Write the sitemap, content model and style guide, and set up Variables in Webflow.
Build at least 4 static pages and 1 Collection template page, with a filtered Collection List on the home page.
Make every page responsive across the four main breakpoints and test on a real phone.
Run the pre-launch checklist: PageSpeed Insights before and after, accessibility checks, form test, page titles and meta descriptions.
Write a one-page case study, a pricing proposal with inclusions, exclusions and milestones, and a 90-day plan for your niche.
evidence: Published webflow.io (or custom domain) link to the complete site
Screenshot of the CMS Collection fields and the Navigator tree
QA sheet with PageSpeed scores and the completed pre-launch checklist
